title: Psychological Safety
subtitle: What happens after someone asks a question, admits a mistake or disagrees, and how to make that moment useful
summary: A useful question can improve the work, yet asking it can carry a social risk. This course builds psychological safety as the readings define it: a team's shared expectation that asking, admitting an error, raising a concern or disagreeing will be examined rather than ridiculed or punished. It is not comfort, niceness or lower standards. You practice raising a precise question, receiving one about your own work, handling a mistake in the present and learning from it, leading repair when you hold more power, and knowing where team habits end and formal routes begin. A workplace simulation lets you try these moves when a newer colleague's question gets brushed aside in a team huddle.
objectives: Explain psychological safety as a shared team expectation about interpersonal risk, and say what it is not: comfort, agreement, lower standards or a promise of secrecy.
Describe how position, earlier responses and different meanings of speaking up can change the cost of a question, without inferring anyone's experience from a group.
Raise a concern as an observation, a task consequence and a specific request, and receive a question about your own work by examining it before defending it.
Respond to a mistake by addressing the present need first, then examining conditions and choices without public blame or promises that no one is responsible.
Distinguish team learning from respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination routes, including the immediate reporting duty of managers and supervisors under Policy 1436.

narrator.voice_notes: Warm, direct colleague who has held back questions and brushed off a few, and learned from both. Steady pace, short sentences, plain words. Curious, never lecturing or grading. Quoted dialogue in a slightly more conversational tone. Confirm the pronunciation of Edmondson before recording.

hero.alt: A newer team member points to a note on a whiteboard and raises a concern while the team lead steps back to listen.

segments.title: Why an ordinary question carries risk

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Psychological Safety. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer with a warm, open expression, hands loosely clasped.
on_screen: What happens after someone asks, admits a mistake or disagrees
scenes.narration: Welcome. Think about the last time you had a question at work and held it back. Maybe you worried you would look unprepared. Maybe the person you would be questioning had more experience, or more say over your next assignment. Maybe the meeting was moving fast, and nobody else seemed confused. Holding back felt reasonable. Most people have done it. This course is about that moment, and about the moment right after someone does speak up. Psychological safety is about what people expect will happen when they ask a question, admit a mistake, raise a concern or disagree. It is not about being nice or comfortable. It is about whether useful information can reach the work. You will look at what the idea means, why the risk is not the same for everyone, and how to raise and receive a question. Then you will step into a workplace simulation where your choices shape what happens next.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What does the first response teach? The two quoted lines appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, turned slightly toward the quotes, one hand raised toward the second line.
on_screen: What does the first response teach?
“Could this instruction leave someone without a usable route?”
scenes.narration: Here is a small exchange from one of the readings behind this course. A colleague asks, “Could this instruction leave someone without a usable route?” The reply is, “We have already discussed that.” Nothing dramatic happened. Yet look at what the reply does. It says a discussion took place. It does not say what that discussion settled. The colleague may need a reference, a correction or a clearer answer. Instead, the reply mostly discourages asking again. If questions keep getting replies like that, people may stop offering the uncertainty the work needs. The reading is careful here. That is a possible pattern, not proof of how everyone feels. So start with the specific response, and the work question it leaves open.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Silence has a cost. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer, one hand open at her side.
scenes.narration: Why does this matter in public service? Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School, is the researcher most associated with the term psychological safety. In her hospital research, the better teams reported more errors, not fewer. They felt able to talk about them. Her work also argues that fear is a poor motivator. It narrows thinking, and it leads people to hold back information that leaders need. Many major failures, in companies and in public organizations, trace back to people who saw a problem and stayed silent. The reading points to human services directly. A case review or an incident debrief that brings problems to the surface, rather than hiding them, matters directly for the safety of the people served. A reflection question from that reading is worth keeping: where would someone hesitate before reporting an error, and what would it cost the person served if they stayed silent?

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Practice problems, practice answers. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, half-turned toward the points.
on_screen: How disagreement and mistakes are handled
Who carries repair, and whether input changes anything
scenes.narration: This is not only a research topic. One reading reports that staff in the Disability Services Division described limited psychological safety, performance pressure, and doubt that their input changes decisions. The reading calls those practice problems with practice answers. That framing matters. It means the answer is not to find braver employees. It is to change what happens when people speak. How is disagreement handled? How are mistakes treated? Who carries the repair when something lands badly? And does anyone's input actually change anything? Those are things other people can see. They are also things you can practice, whatever your role.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: The path ahead. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand open toward the list.
on_screen: What it is, and why the risk differs
Asking, receiving, mistakes and formal routes
scenes.narration: Here is the path ahead. First, what psychological safety is and is not. Then why speaking up costs some people more than others. Next, how to raise a precise question, and how to receive one about your own work. After that, mistakes and repair. Finally, where team habits end and formal routes begin. Each part closes with a few questions to think over, alone or with a colleague you trust. Before you go on, bring one real moment to mind. A time you held a question back, or a time someone questioned you. Keep it with you as you go.

check.prompt: A colleague asks whether an instruction could leave someone without a usable route. The reply is, “We have already discussed that.” What does the reply leave open?

options.text: It says a discussion happened but not what it settled, so the colleague's work question is still unanswered and the next person may think twice before asking.

feedback.text: You kept the work question in view and noticed what the reply teaches. Build on that by asking what the earlier discussion actually established.
Next time you hear a reply like that, try: “What did that discussion settle? I want to make sure this case is covered.”

options.text: Very little, since the team already talked it through, and reopening old discussions every time someone asks can slow the work down for everyone else in the meeting.

feedback.text: Protecting meeting time is a real concern, and repeating old debates can drain a team. The catch is that the reply never showed what the earlier talk decided, so the question stays open.
From the asker's side, the reply can sound like the question itself was the problem. A one-line pointer to what was decided would answer it and save time.

options.text: It shows the person who replied does not care about access, so that attitude should be raised with their supervisor before the instruction itself is looked at.

feedback.text: The reply shows a brush-off, not a motive. A stronger response stays with what can be seen: the question is unanswered. That keeps attention on the instruction.
What would you need to see before concluding what someone cares about?

reflection: Think of a question you held back at work. What did you expect would happen if you asked it?
What reply have you heard, or given, that answered a question with a shortcut instead of an explanation?
Where in your work could an unasked question become a problem for the people you serve?

segments.title: What psychological safety is and is not

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A shared belief about risk. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands relaxed at his sides.
on_screen: A team condition, not a personality trait
scenes.narration: Edmondson defined team psychological safety as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Interpersonal risks are ordinary work acts that could make someone look ignorant, incompetent or disruptive. Asking a question. Admitting a mistake. Raising a concern. Disagreeing with someone more senior. Notice two things about that definition. First, it is shared. It describes how a group works, not how confident one person is. Second, it is about expectations: what people believe will happen if they take that small risk. So the question is not whether someone is naturally bold. The question is how the team responds when someone takes an ordinary work risk.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What the research shows. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, gesturing toward the first point.
scenes.narration: Her 1999 study looked at fifty-one work teams in a manufacturing company. Psychological safety was associated with more learning behavior, such as asking for help, discussing errors and raising uncertainty. Learning behavior, in turn, was associated with better team performance. The readings are careful about what that means. The study shows association, not proof that one causes the other. The pattern has appeared in many settings since. Still, it does not certify any team at DHS, and it is not a way to diagnose an employee. Think of it as a useful lens for looking at how your team handles uncertainty.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Not niceness, not low standards. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand raised slightly, palm out.
on_screen: Candor is how standards get met
scenes.narration: Here is the most common misunderstanding. Psychological safety is not being nice, avoiding conflict or lowering expectations. Edmondson's goal is high safety combined with high expectations. A team can hold a demanding standard and still make it safe to say that something is not working. In fact, candor is what lets high standards be met. Her book describes candid organizations, such as the film studio Pixar, as demanding rather than comfortable. In her account, candor is how quality gets made. Discomfort is normal when people learn. The real question is whether speaking up gets punished or humiliated. Leaders, in her account, still sanction clear violations. Safety and accountability sit together.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A calm meeting proves little. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, head tilted slightly, thoughtful.
on_screen: Agreement is not evidence of safety
scenes.narration: A smooth meeting can feel like a good sign. Nobody objects. Everyone nods. But the readings warn that a meeting with no questions may reflect clarity, a missed opportunity, or worry about the response. The record alone cannot tell you which. Agreement is useful when it is supported. It does not show how the team would handle a challenge. The opposite is also true. A hard conversation does not mean learning is impossible. So do not use calm as proof, and do not use conflict as proof either. Look at what actually happens to a question when someone asks it.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Disagreement is not disrespect. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, holding up two fingers as if counting two separate questions.
scenes.narration: A team needs room to challenge a conclusion without the challenge being treated as misconduct. Minnesota Management and Budget's Respectful Workplace policy, Policy 1432, draws the same line. It separates respectful disagreement and normal professional supervision from disrespectful conduct, such as shouting, threats, bullying or demeaning treatment. That gives you two questions to keep apart. Is the claim supported by evidence? And was the exchange respectful? A colleague can be wrong and respectful. A colleague can be right and still speak to someone in a demeaning way. Each question gets its own answer, and neither one cancels the other.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What it does not promise. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, shaking his head gently, a slight smile.
on_screen: Not secrecy, not freedom from accountability
scenes.narration: Sometimes a leader tries to build safety by promising too much. Every idea will be accepted. Nothing said here will ever leave this room. Nobody will be held accountable. Those promises sound welcoming. The readings say they go beyond both the concept and anyone's authority. Ideas still need evidence. Some concerns a supervisor has to route formally, such as an allegation of discrimination. Accountability still applies. A more honest invitation sounds like this: “Raise questions here. Here is what is still open, who decides, and what has to go through another process.” That is less dramatic. It is also much easier to believe. The readings add one more distinction. Cultural safety, a team's ability to raise concerns, and an organization's systems for reporting and responding are related, but different. One survey or one session does not measure all three.

check.prompt: Which statement fits psychological safety as the readings describe it?

options.text: A team expects that asking, admitting an error or disagreeing will not bring humiliation, while standards, evidence and formal duties all stay in place.

feedback.text: You held both halves together: room to take an ordinary risk, and standards that still apply. Build on it by noticing which half your team tends to drop under pressure.
On your team, what usually happens to the first person who disagrees?

options.text: A team where people feel comfortable and conflict stays low, because members trust each other enough that hard feedback is rarely needed to get the work done well.

feedback.text: Many people picture safety as comfort, and a calm team can feel safe. The readings frame it differently: safety makes hard feedback possible rather than unnecessary.
Compare this with high safety and high expectations. A team can be candid and demanding at once. Low conflict on its own says little about what happens to a question.

options.text: A promise from the leader that every concern raised inside the team stays inside the team, so people can speak without worrying about what might follow.

feedback.text: That promise goes beyond any leader's authority. Some concerns a supervisor has to route formally. A stronger invitation explains what is open and what has to go elsewhere.
Picture the person who later learns their concern had to be reported after all. An honest limit at the start would have served them better than a promise.

options.text: A trait that confident employees bring with them, which is why some people on a team speak up easily in meetings while others usually stay quiet.

feedback.text: Edmondson describes a team condition, not a personality trait. The useful question is how the team responds to a risk, not who is naturally bold.
When someone is quiet, try looking at the conditions first: how was the last question received, and was there another way to contribute?

reflection: Think of a team where you felt free to disagree. What did the leader or the group do that made that possible?
Where have you seen kindness used as a reason to skip hard feedback?
What promise about safety have you heard that went further than anyone could keep?

segments.title: Why the risk is not the same for everyone

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: The cost of asking differs. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands loosely clasped.
on_screen: Silence is not evidence of no concern
scenes.narration: The same invitation can land very differently on two people in the same room. A senior employee and someone in their first month may both hear, “Any questions?” Their position and their past experience differ, so the risk feels different. The readings name several things that shape that risk. Position. How earlier questions were received. How visible the person is. What support they can reach. None of that creates a rule about any one person. It does mean you should not read someone's confidence, experience or agreement from silence alone. And repeatedly asking the least secure person to be braver can leave the real conditions unchanged.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: An open door is not enough. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one arm extended slightly as if holding a door open.
on_screen: An open door is not enough
The person inviting input may control assignments
Pair the door with usable routes
scenes.narration: Many leaders say their door is always open. That statement helps only when what happens next supports it. The person who invites input may also control assignments, evaluations and development. Staff can reasonably weigh those consequences before disagreeing. In one reading's practice case, a temporary staff member sees an access problem in a form. She expects that challenging the project lead in public could harm her future assignments. A prepared written route, or a private conversation, may make that contribution usable. It should not require her to explain her personal history. And a lack of visitors through the open door does not show that no concerns exist.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Who bears the cost. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, serious and calm, hands at her sides.
on_screen: A climate that punishes candor silences some people first
scenes.narration: The Fearless Organization reading adds a point about inclusion. Staff from underrepresented groups often bear the highest cost for speaking up. So a climate that punishes candor tends to silence them first. The same reading notes a common critique. Edmondson's framework says little about how power and identity shape who feels safe. Her later writing addresses this, the reading notes, but practitioners should still add an equity lens. Here is the guardrail. This is about conditions on a team, not about what any one person feels. You cannot know someone's experience from a group they belong to. The reading asks whether people from different identity groups experience the same level of safety on your team, and how you would find out. Finding out is the point. Guessing is not.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two ways of caring. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, both hands open, one slightly higher than the other, as if weighing two things.
on_screen: A quick question can be active care
A prepared question can be respect
scenes.narration: One reading tells a practice story about two colleagues reviewing a draft. One asks questions right away, as the draft is read aloud. The other wants to review the wording first and send a prepared question. At first, each misreads the other. The quick questioner sees the delay as reluctance to challenge the team. The careful preparer sees the quick questions as putting colleagues on the spot. Then each explains what their habit means to them. For one, asking right away showed care: you name a problem while others can still fix it together. For the other, arriving with a considered question respected everyone's preparation and the relationship. Both cared about the work. Those meanings belonged to those two people, who chose to share them. Neither one speaks for a group.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Widen the frame, then change the response. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, gesturing outward with both hands.
on_screen: Widen the frame, then change the response
Offer more than one way in
scenes.narration: The lesson is not to list styles or ask people to be tolerant. It is to change what you do. Make the open question visible. Let people raise it in the room, or send a prepared question in time for the decision. Then check that the written route actually reaches the person responsible before the choice closes. A comment box nobody reads is not a real option. Moving someone's contribution out of the room and then forgetting it keeps the look of choice while losing the knowledge. Privately, notice which signal you tend to reward. Speed. Certainty. Preparation. Direct challenge. Each one can be a form of care.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Contribution without disclosure. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand resting lightly over her heart.
on_screen: No one speaks for a whole group
scenes.narration: One more guardrail. A person should not have to share a personal history, or explain an experience of exclusion, before their question is taken seriously. Nor should anyone be asked to speak for a whole community, or to carry the work of educating others because of who they are. A practical concern about a form or a process can stand on its own. Ask for evidence and perspective, not identity stories. If someone chooses to share more, receive it with care and keep it with them.

check.prompt: A newer colleague rarely speaks in team meetings but sends careful written questions afterward. Which response fits the readings best?

options.text: Make sure written questions reach the person deciding before the choice closes, and do not read the colleague's quiet in meetings as low confidence or commitment.

feedback.text: You treated the written questions as real contributions and made sure they can still matter. Build on it by telling the team when written input is due and who reads it.
To the colleague, a prepared question may be the respectful way to contribute. Seeing it reach the decision tells them the route is real.

options.text: Encourage the colleague to raise questions in the room next time, since live questions get discussed by everyone and their good ideas deserve more visibility on the team.

feedback.text: Wanting a colleague's good ideas to be seen is generous. The catch is that it makes speaking in the room the measure of contribution, and the written route already works.
A stronger response changes the arrangement instead of the person: written questions reach the decision in time, and live questions stay welcome too.

options.text: Ask the colleague what in their background makes speaking in meetings hard for them, so the team can adjust the way it runs meetings to fit their culture better.

feedback.text: This asks for a personal story and assumes the reason is cultural. A stronger move asks what would make contributing easier, without needing to know why.
Try instead: “Your written questions have been useful. Is there anything about how the team takes input that would make it easier for you?”

reflection: Who on your team has the most influence over other people's assignments? How might that shape what gets said in the room?
Which signal of engagement do you tend to reward: speed, certainty, preparation or direct challenge?
If you wanted to know whether everyone on your team can raise concerns equally, how would you find out without guessing?

segments.title: Raising a question and receiving one

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Make the question examinable. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the royal blue blouse (C5), playing the team member in the reading's story, stands full length, holding a printed page and pointing to a line on it.
on_screen: “This paragraph names only the web contact.”
scenes.narration: When you raise a concern, precision helps the work. One reading offers a simple shape. Name what you observed. Explain how it could affect the task. Ask for what you need. In the reading's practice story, a team member notices that the current source lists two contact options, while a draft notice lists only the web contact. She first considers saying, “You are hiding the access problem.” That adds a motive the material does not show. Instead she says, “This paragraph names only the web contact. The current source includes another option. Which one applies to this notice?” The second version gives the person responsible something concrete to check, instead of a character to defend.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Honest about what you do not know. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand raised slightly in a modest, open gesture.
on_screen: Honest about what you do not know
Precision helps; polish is not the price of an answer
scenes.narration: You can name your uncertainty honestly. “I may be missing a condition” invites a check without giving up the concern. That is different from an apology that erases the question: “Sorry, I am probably wrong, so ignore this.” Neither inflated certainty nor self-dismissal makes the evidence stronger. And precision should never become an entry fee. A person under pressure may not phrase a concern neatly. If you are on the receiving end, hear the substance and ask a clarifying question. “This instruction names no contact” is easier to examine than “Nobody cares.” But someone who says the second one may still have found something real.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Within your role. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand gesturing to the side as if passing something along.
on_screen: Bring the question to the person responsible
You do not have to become the final authority
scenes.narration: Choose a realistic route. If the person responsible for the draft is in the meeting, point to the paragraph there. If another role must interpret the condition, help bring the question to that role. You do not need to quietly become the final policy authority, or promise a correction you cannot approve. Clear responsibility for receiving the question matters more than copying a long list of people on a message. And this is worth saying plainly. Better wording is not your job alone. A precise question can still meet a poor response. How the team receives questions matters just as much as how you ask them.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: When someone questions your work. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the white blouse with curly hair (C3), playing the experienced colleague in the reading's story, stands full length, holding a thick folder against her chest, mid-thought.
on_screen: “What next step does it suggest to you?”
scenes.narration: Now flip it. Someone questions your work. In another practice story, an experienced colleague has prepared a careful draft. A new colleague asks whether one sentence explains the next contact step accurately. The experienced colleague feels the effort behind the draft is being overlooked. She starts to say, “You would understand if you had been here longer.” The draft may well be sound. But that reply puts length of service where the evidence should be. A more useful opening is, “Thanks for pointing to that sentence. What next step does it suggest to you?” That gathers how the sentence actually reads, so it can be compared with the source.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Recognition is not agreement. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, counting on his fingers.
on_screen: A receipt is not an answer
scenes.narration: Taking a question seriously does not mean agreeing with it. You can thank the person, check the source, and then explain why the wording is accurate. Or you can change it through the proper review. Or you can name a condition that another role has to settle. The value is in examining it. A warm “Great question,” followed by no look at the sentence, leaves both the work gap and the interpersonal gap in place. Make the answer usable. Tell the person what you found, or who is checking and how the answer will come back. A note that says “received” is not the same thing as an answer.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Do not ask for reassurance. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, hands in a calm, steady position at his waist.
on_screen: Good intentions do not answer the question
No loyalty test before the work
scenes.narration: One last trap. When a question feels personal, it is tempting to defend your good intention, or to ask the other person to confirm that everything is fine. But your intention to help does not answer whether the instruction worked. If that defense becomes a habit, colleagues learn that feedback mainly creates a need to comfort the receiver. Do not make agreement, loyalty or a personal story the price of getting a question examined. Privately, notice what you hear when someone questions your work. Does a sign of status or preparation make the question sound like disrespect? Asking one clarifying question before you explain is a small practice that changes a lot.

check.prompt: A new colleague asks whether a sentence in your draft explains the next contact step correctly. You are fairly sure it does. What is the most useful first response?

options.text: Thank them for pointing to the sentence, ask what next step it suggests to them, and compare it with the current source before you explain what you find.

feedback.text: You stayed open even though you expected to be right. That keeps the question about the sentence, not about either of you. Build on it by telling them what you found.
If the source backs you up, try: “Here is the condition it follows. Does that make the sentence clearer, or should the wording change?”

options.text: Walk them through the background behind the wording and how long the team has used it, so they can see why the sentence reads the way it does now.

feedback.text: Explaining the background is a natural, helpful instinct, especially with someone new. The gap is that history shows how the sentence came to be, not whether it reads clearly today.
A stronger first move asks how the sentence reads to them. Then the background can answer the actual confusion instead of a guessed one.

options.text: Tell them it is a great question and you appreciate them speaking up, then keep the sentence as written, since you are fairly sure it is right.

feedback.text: The thanks is warm, but the sentence never gets examined. Recognition works best as the start of a check, not a replacement for one.
To the new colleague, praise followed by no change and no explanation can feel like a polite way of closing the door.

options.text: Change the sentence right away to match their reading, since a new person's confusion is enough evidence that the wording is not working for anyone reading it.

feedback.text: Welcoming the question does not settle its answer. A stronger move checks the source first, then changes the wording if the check supports it.
What would you want to know before deciding the sentence is wrong for everyone?

reflection: Think of a concern you raised that turned into a debate about motives. How could you have named only what you observed?
When someone questions your work, what is your first reaction? What clarifying question could you ask before explaining?
Where have you seen a friendly acknowledgment stand in for an actual answer?

segments.title: Mistakes and repair

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A mistake needs a present response. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer, steady and calm.
on_screen: A mistake needs a present response
Correct it, then examine how it happened
scenes.narration: Mistakes are where psychological safety is tested hardest. Picture a service message that goes out with the wrong date. The readings say to keep two needs in view. First, the present problem. The date may need correcting right away, by the person responsible for the message. Second, the learning question. How did the wrong date get in, and how did it get past review? Calling the employee careless can hide a confusing source or a missed review step. Saying mistakes never matter ignores the effect on the people who read the message. A thoughtful response handles the current problem first, then asks a specific learning question.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A future meeting cannot fix today. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the navy polo (C4), playing the team member in the reading's story, stands full length, holding a large envelope, looking at it with a slight frown.
on_screen: A future meeting cannot fix today
Supply what the receiver needs now
scenes.narration: In another practice story, a team member sends a review package without its source attachment. The receiver cannot check a condition and sends it back. The team member offers to talk about the mistake at the next team learning meeting. Reflection may help, but it does not supply the missing attachment. Start with what the work needs now. Then look at how it happened. In the story, the package checklist covered the draft but not its source. The sender also assumed the receiver could find the source alone. A specific fix might add the source to the checklist. A promise never to make a mistake again offers certainty that nobody can deliver.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two shortcuts to avoid. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand lifted toward each point in turn.
scenes.narration: Under pressure, teams often reach for one of two shortcuts. One is public blame. Name the person and move on. That can produce a quick explanation. It also discourages people from disclosing errors, and it can hide a gap in the process. The other shortcut is to declare that nobody is responsible, because the system caused it. That can make disclosure easier for a moment. But it goes beyond a leader's authority, and it can leave the next task with no owner. The readings describe a third path: learning with boundaries. Correct the work. Examine conditions and choices together. Keep any formal matter, such as a personnel question, in its own route.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Repair sits with more power. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, serious, hands loosely clasped in front.
on_screen: No explaining or forgiving on a schedule
scenes.narration: Some mistakes are not about documents. They are about how someone was treated. One reading puts it directly. When a comment or decision lands badly, the person with more power leads the repair. The leader names it and takes responsibility. The person harmed should not have to explain, educate or forgive on a schedule. Most awkward moments come from not knowing, and the fitting response is information and a chance to change. A lack of knowledge does not erase harm, though. And it does not decide whether a formal reporting process applies. Intentional harm goes to the formal channels.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Repair in the same setting. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8), playing the supervisor in the reading's story, stands full length, facing the viewer as if addressing a team, one hand open.
on_screen: Credit the concern and say you should have listened
scenes.narration: Here is a practice case from the readings. A supervisor of a policy team dismisses a newer analyst's concern that a notice will confuse families. There is no time to revisit it, she says. Two weeks later, a county partner raises the same problem. The supervisor notices the analyst has stopped speaking in meetings. What now? Telling him privately to speak up more puts the burden back on him. Waiting for him to raise it puts repair on the person with less power. The reading's stronger response: at the next team meeting, she says he raised this first, that she should have listened, what will change in the notice, and how she will handle concerns from now on. That works because his concern was raised in an open meeting. If someone raised a concern privately, ask them before you credit them in front of others.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Repair your own response. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand on her chest, the other open toward the viewer.
on_screen: Check where your first reading traveled
scenes.narration: You do not have to be a supervisor to repair a response. If you brushed off a colleague's question, you can say so. “My reply cut off a relevant question. Here is how it will get an answer now.” That is more useful than asking the colleague to confirm that everything is fine. An apology can matter without settling what the other person experienced. Also check where your first reading traveled. Did it end up in a note, a summary, or someone's view of a colleague's ability? A private change of mind may not fix a label that has already moved. Correct what you can, within your role.

check.prompt: A teammate realizes a notice went out with an outdated date. The team lead wants to handle it well. Which response fits the readings best?

options.text: Correct the date through the person responsible now, then look at how the old date got in and past review, keeping any formal matter separate.

feedback.text: You put the people reading the notice first, then made room to learn. Build on that by picking one specific step to change and checking whether it helps next time.
For the teammate, seeing the problem fixed and the process examined, rather than their character, makes it easier to speak up the next time something slips.

options.text: Put the error on the agenda for next month's team learning review, so the whole team can examine it together without anyone feeling singled out in the moment.

feedback.text: Wanting to learn as a team without singling anyone out is a good instinct. The catch is timing: the people who got the wrong date need a correction now, not next month.
Try doing both: correct the notice today, then bring the how-it-happened question to the review.

options.text: Reassure the teammate that nobody is responsible because the process caused it, so that people across the team feel safe admitting mistakes in the future.

feedback.text: The process may have played a part, but declaring that nobody is responsible goes beyond what a lead can promise and can leave the fix with no owner.
How could you name the process gap and still keep the next step owned by someone?

options.text: Name the teammate in the team meeting so the cause is clear, then ask everyone to check their work more carefully from now on.

feedback.text: Public blame gives a quick explanation but can hide the step that let the date through. A stronger response corrects the notice and examines the review process.
Everyone else in the meeting learns something too: that admitting an error gets you named in front of the team.

reflection: When a mistake surfaces on your team, which shortcut is more tempting: blame, or declaring that nobody is responsible?
Think of a time your response cut someone off. Where did that first reading travel, and could any of it still be corrected?
Where do you hold more power than the people around you, and what would leading a repair look like there?

segments.title: Team habits and formal routes

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three layers. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand held flat, raised in steps as if marking levels.
on_screen: Law sets the floor; policy sets a higher standard
You do not have to classify it first
scenes.narration: Psychological safety makes it more likely that people raise problems early. It does not replace formal routes, and it does not make anyone an investigator. The respectful workplace reading separates three layers. Federal and Minnesota law set the floor for illegal harassment and discrimination. State policy sets a higher standard for daily conduct. Policy 1436 covers unwelcome conduct tied to a protected class, including offensive jokes, slurs, deliberately misgendering someone, and deliberately mispronouncing their name. Policy 1432 covers disrespect that is not tied to a protected class, such as shouting, bullying or demeaning treatment. Here is the practical point. You do not have to decide which layer something fits before you raise it. Sorting that out belongs to Human Resources and the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: If you see it happen. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand open, fingers spread as if counting five.
on_screen: Ask the targeted person what they want
scenes.narration: If you see disrespect or harassment happen, you have options. Right To Be, a national nonprofit, teaches five of them, known as the five Ds. Distract: interrupt the moment, perhaps with a work question or a short break. Delegate: bring in someone with more authority, such as a supervisor or a meeting chair. Document: make a factual note of what happened. Delay: check in afterward, say it was not okay, and ask what the person needs. Direct: name the behavior briefly, but only when it is safe and likely to help. With any note you make, ask the targeted person what they want done with it, and do not share it without their permission, unless you are a supervisor with a duty to report. Delay is often the most underused option. It leaves the targeted person in control of what happens next.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: If someone brings you a concern. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, leaning in slightly, listening.
on_screen: If someone brings you a concern
Listen, thank them, share the routes
scenes.narration: If a colleague brings you a concern, listen and thank them. Do not judge whether it is serious enough. Be honest about what you can and cannot keep confidential. Then share the routes. A supervisor. Human Resources. The Equal Opportunity and Access Division. A union representative. The Employee Assistance Program. And agencies outside DHS, such as the Minnesota Department of Human Rights or the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Do not interview other people or try to work out what happened. Route the concern; do not investigate it. And watch for retaliation. No one may be punished for reporting, for opposing harassment or discrimination, or for taking part in an investigation. Retaliation can be obvious, like a worse assignment, or subtle, like being left out of meetings.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: If you supervise or manage. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, upright and serious, hands at his sides.
on_screen: No reassurance or repair comes first
scenes.narration: If you are a manager or supervisor, there is a specific duty. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, and follow agency procedures. DHS policy directs supervisors to refer these complaints to the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, and not to investigate them. That means no interviewing witnesses, no asking the person to prove what happened, no confronting the person accused, and no mediating. You cannot agree to keep protected-class harassment secret. And a team conversation, an apology or an attempt at repair can never delay that report. Repair may matter later. It is never a gate.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Invite before the decision closes. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand raised beside him as if holding a calendar page.
on_screen: Name what is open and who decides
Ask for the strongest case against your idea
scenes.narration: Back to everyday team habits. Edmondson's toolkit for leaders has three parts. Set the stage by framing the work as uncertain and tying it to purpose. Invite participation through humility, inquiry and structured forums. Respond productively by appreciating input, removing the stigma from failure, and still sanctioning clear violations. In practice, “Any questions?” at the end of a meeting is often too broad and too late. A useful invitation names what is being decided, what is still uncertain, who decides, and how people can respond before the choice closes. One reading adds a simple habit: before deciding, ask for the strongest case against your own idea. Her book adds one more point. A leader's reaction to the first person who speaks up shapes whether anyone else will.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Show what changed. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand open toward the points, relaxed.
on_screen: Say what changed because someone spoke up
scenes.narration: An invitation is only a beginning. People watch what happens next. Did the question get an answer? Did the answer address what was asked? One reading suggests a regular habit. Say what changed because someone spoke up, and if nothing did, say why. You do not have to agree with every suggestion. What helps is a useful account of how the question was considered. The same reading adds: watch the grind. Constant urgency silences people. Protect time for thinking, and for saying no. Thank people who raise concerns, in a way that respects their preferences. Public thanks may be welcome. It should never expose someone who raised a concern privately.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Evidence, not a safety score. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, thoughtful, one hand at his chin.
on_screen: Do not rank people by how often they speak
scenes.narration: Finally, be careful how you judge progress. Fewer questions could mean clearer instructions, less opportunity, or reluctance to ask. More concerns could mean the route works better, or that a new problem appeared. A count alone cannot settle it. Avoid ranking people by how often they speak, and avoid labels for a quiet colleague. Describe what actually happened. Which questions got answers. Which are still open. What one person told you, kept to its own scope. What nobody has said stays unknown. That kind of honest, mixed account gives the next conversation something real to build on.

check.prompt: You do not supervise anyone. A colleague on another team tells you a teammate keeps joking about their accommodation in front of others. They ask you to keep it between the two of you. What fits best?

options.text: Thank them, say the jokes are not okay, describe routes such as their supervisor, Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, and ask what they want next.

feedback.text: You took it seriously, kept the decision with the person, and made the routes concrete. Build on it by offering to go with them if they choose to report. If you supervise or manage, the answer changes: you report it right away, and you tell them that honestly.
If they choose to tell their supervisor, it helps to mention honestly that a supervisor has to report a concern like this right away.

options.text: Write down what they told you and send it to Human Resources yourself today, so the concern reaches people who can act on it before anything like it happens again.

feedback.text: Wanting it to reach someone who can act is a caring instinct. As a colleague without a supervisor's duty, though, sending it without asking takes the choice away from the person it happened to.
A stronger response shares the routes and asks what they want. Your note can support them, if and when they decide to use it.

options.text: Talk with the teammate yourself and ask what happened, so you can tell whether the jokes were meant to hurt before anyone decides to involve Human Resources.

feedback.text: Finding out what happened is investigating, and it belongs to the people responsible for that process. It can also expose the colleague who confided in you.
Whose decision is it whether the teammate hears about this, and when?

options.text: Agree to keep it between the two of you, since it is their experience to handle, and check in with them next week to see whether the jokes have stopped.

feedback.text: Honoring their request is respectful, and as a peer you can keep it private. What it leaves out is the routes, which are what make their choice a real one.
A stronger response keeps it private and still names the routes, so the decision stays with them and is an informed one.

reflection: If someone brought you a concern tomorrow, would you know which routes to share? What would you need to look up first?
Which of the five Ds feels most natural to you, and which feels hardest?
When did you last hear someone say what changed because a colleague spoke up? What would it take to make that a habit?

simulations.intro: Whatever your job at DHS, you have probably sat in a meeting where someone asked a question and the room moved on. In this scenario, I want you to sit at a small team table as a peer, not the lead. You do not supervise anyone, so your influence comes from what you notice, what you say, and how you handle your own mistakes. Watch for the moments when one short reply decides whether the next person speaks.
simulations.title: The Monday huddle
simulations.learner_role: You are a member of a small DHS team that keeps a quick-reference guide up to date. Call-line colleagues use the guide when people ask where to send documents and whom to call. You are a peer on the team and do not supervise anyone. Your teammates include the team lead, who supervises the team and decides what goes into the guide, an experienced colleague who has worked on it for years, and a newer team member who joined six weeks ago.
simulations.background: This team's practice is a twenty-minute huddle every Monday to review changes to the guide. This week the agenda is full and the team lead is keeping an eye on the clock. Last week you updated the contacts section of the guide yourself. The call-line lead, who supervises the colleagues answering calls, is not in the huddle but relies on the guide every day. The team also holds a monthly learning review, where it looks at mistakes together.

decisions.setup: Halfway through the huddle, the newer team member asks, “The guide says to transfer these callers to the program line, but the new training sheet says to take a message and call back. Which one applies?” The experienced colleague answers before anyone else: “Everyone else understands it. You're overthinking it.” A couple of people laugh. The team lead glances at the clock and starts to say, “Okay, next item.” The newer team member looks down at his notes.
decisions.prompt: What do you do in this moment?

choices.text: “Before we move on, can we look at that? I'm not sure how those two fit either. If they conflict, callers could get different answers. Who can confirm which one applies?”
choices.consequence: The team lead pauses. The experienced colleague says, a little stiffly, “It's covered.” Then she reads the two lines side by side and stops. “Actually, they don't match. The training sheet changed last month.” The team lead asks the newer team member which calls he had in mind and says he will check with the person responsible for the training sheet and bring the answer back by Friday. The newer team member writes that down and, for the first time in the huddle, looks up.

feedback.text: You brought the question back to the work and admitted your own uncertainty, which made it easier for others to look again. Build on it by checking on Friday that the answer actually reached the guide.
From the newer team member's seat, a laugh and a quick “next item” can feel like a verdict on him. Hearing a peer say “I'm not sure either” changes what the question means in the room.
A short version works when time is tight: “Can we take thirty seconds on that? Who can confirm which one applies?”

choices.text: Say nothing now, since the huddle is short and the team lead is already moving on, and catch the newer team member afterward to walk him through how the two instructions fit together.
choices.consequence: The team lead moves to the next item. The newer team member stops taking notes. Nobody comes back to the two instructions. The experienced colleague's comment hangs in the room for a moment, and the next two agenda items go quickly, with no questions from anyone.

feedback.text: Not wanting to put him further on the spot is a kind instinct, and huddles really are short. The catch is that his question is about the guide, so a private chat leaves the work exactly where it was.
A stronger move keeps the question in the room for a moment and asks who can confirm the answer. Then the follow-up afterward can be about him, not about rescuing his question.
If you had asked that question and the room moved on, what would you conclude about asking the next one?

choices.text: “I think it's in last month's huddle notes. I can send you the link after this so you have it, and that way the team lead can keep the huddle on schedule.”
choices.consequence: The experienced colleague nods. The team lead says, “Great,” and moves on. The newer team member says a quiet “Thanks.” Nobody has said whether the two instructions actually fit together, and the guide still tells callers one thing while the training sheet says another.

feedback.text: Pointing to a resource is helpful, but the notes may not answer whether the two instructions conflict. A stronger move asks who can confirm which applies, so the guide gets checked.
Keeping a huddle on schedule matters, and offering a link feels like a fair compromise. It does, though, quietly agree that the question was already settled.
To the call-line colleagues using both documents, the open question is not old news. It decides what they tell the next caller.

choices.text: “Good catch. The training sheet is newer, so the guide must be out of date. Let's change the guide to match it today so callers get the right instruction.”
choices.consequence: The newer team member looks relieved. The experienced colleague folds her arms. “The training sheet could just as easily be the one that's wrong.” The team lead agrees that nobody has checked yet and says he will ask the person responsible for the training sheet which instruction applies before anything in the guide changes. The question is on the table now, though the huddle has gotten a little tense.

feedback.text: You kept the question alive, which matters. The gap is that welcoming a question does not settle its answer. A stronger move asks who can confirm which one applies before anything changes.
To the experienced colleague, a quick verdict against the guide can feel like her years of work were dismissed in one sentence, which makes her less likely to examine it openly.
Try pairing support with a check: “That's a real question. I don't know which is current. Who can confirm before we change anything?”

decisions.setup: A few minutes later, the team lead reaches the end of the agenda. “Anything else before we close?” Nobody speaks. The two instructions still have not been checked against each other, and call-line colleagues are using both. The newer team member is closing his laptop.
decisions.prompt: Do you say anything before the huddle ends?

choices.text: “Before we close, can we go back to the two instructions? I'm not sure they match, and callers are using both. Who could check which one callers should get?”
choices.consequence: The room is quiet for a second. Then the team lead says, “Fair point,” and asks the newer team member which calls he meant. The experienced colleague reads both lines and admits they do not match. The team lead says he will check with the person responsible for the training sheet and bring the answer back by Friday. It took one more sentence to bring the question back.

feedback.text: You used the last open moment to return the question to the work, and you shared the uncertainty instead of leaving it with him. Build on it by asking sooner next time, while the question is still warm.
For the newer team member, hearing his question come back from someone else may matter more than any private reassurance would.

choices.text: Let the huddle close on time, then send the newer team member a friendly message: “Don't take that comment personally. You'll pick this up fast. Ask me anything, anytime, okay?”
choices.consequence: The newer team member replies, “Thanks.” The two instructions stay as they are. Call-line colleagues keep using both, and the question he raised is now a private conversation instead of a work question.

feedback.text: A kind private message is a very common response, and it may feel good to receive. It also treats the problem as his feelings, when the problem he named is in the guide.
A stronger move brings the question back before the huddle ends, so it gets checked. The private check-in can still follow.
What would tell the newer team member that his question was useful, not just forgivable?

decisions.setup: Tuesday morning, the call-line lead messages you directly. “A caller told us the number in the guide for the document help line is disconnected. Can you check?” You open the guide. Last week you updated that section, and you copied the number from an old contact list in the shared folder. You check the current program page: the number changed months ago. Call-line staff have been reading the old number to callers since Thursday.
decisions.prompt: What do you do?

choices.text: Correct the number now, tell the call-line lead and the team lead what happened, ask whether callers given the old number need follow-up, and flag the old contact list.
choices.consequence: The call-line lead replies within minutes. “Thank you. That helps.” She asks her staff to note any callers who mention the old number so they can be called back. The team lead thanks you for flagging it quickly, takes the old contact list out of the shared folder, and asks you to bring one question to the next huddle: how did an old list end up as a source? Nobody makes it bigger than it is, and nobody pretends it did not happen.

feedback.text: You handled the present need first, told the people who rely on the guide, and pointed at the condition behind the slip. Build on it by suggesting one specific change, such as checking numbers against the current program page.
For the call-line lead, a quick, plain account is what lets her staff fix things for callers. It also tells her the guide's team will say so when something goes wrong.

choices.text: Correct the number right away, check the rest of the contacts section against the program page, and reply to the call-line lead, “Fixed, and I checked the other numbers too.”
choices.consequence: The call-line lead replies with a thumbs-up. The guide is right again within ten minutes, and the other numbers in the contacts section match the program page. The team lead does not know anything happened. Nobody has asked about callers who already have the old number, and the old contact list is still in the shared folder, where anyone updating another section could pull from it.

feedback.text: Fixing it fast and checking the rest of the section is a very natural reaction to your own slip, and both steps are right. What it leaves behind is the callers who already have the old number, and the list that caused it.
A stronger move adds two sentences: what happened, and where the old number came from. That turns a private fix into something the team can learn from.
If a teammate had made this slip, what would you want them to tell the team?

choices.text: Correct the number, then post a long apology in the team chat saying you feel terrible, should have checked, and promise it will never happen again because you will triple-check everything.
choices.consequence: The number is fixed. In the chat, two teammates reply quickly: “Don't be so hard on yourself!” The experienced colleague adds a heart. The call-line lead, who is not in the team chat, still does not know whether callers given the old number need a follow-up. The old contact list is still in the shared folder.

feedback.text: Owning the mistake matters, and you did. The gap is that the apology goes to the team chat, while the call-line lead and the callers still need something specific. A plain account to them would do more.
Feeling terrible about a mistake is human. A promise never to slip again offers a certainty nobody can deliver; one changed step, like checking the program page, can actually be tested.
Try: “I copied the old number from an outdated list. It's fixed. Here's who may need a callback, and here's the list to retire.”

choices.text: Add the error to the team's monthly learning review next week, so the cause gets examined properly with everyone instead of patched in a rush today.
choices.consequence: You add a line to the review agenda. The guide still shows the old number while you wait, and the call-line lead's message sits unanswered.

feedback.text: Wanting the cause examined properly is a good learning instinct. The timing is the problem: callers are being given a disconnected number today, and a meeting next week cannot fix that.
A stronger move corrects the guide and answers the call-line lead now, then brings the how-it-happened question to the review.

decisions.setup: Twenty minutes later, the call-line lead writes again, this time copying the team lead. “Callers have had this number since Thursday. Some may still be waiting on help that isn't coming. Do you know where the number came from, and could it be anywhere else in the guide?”
decisions.prompt: How do you reply?

choices.text: “That's on me: I copied it from an old contact list. I'll make sure the guide is correct now and check other sections. Could your staff note callers who mention it?”
choices.consequence: The call-line lead writes back, “Thanks. That's what we needed.” The team lead replies that he will take the old contact list out of the shared folder and asks you to bring the question of how it got used to the next huddle. Within the hour, the guide is correct and the call-line staff are noting callers who need a follow-up.

feedback.text: You gave a plain account, fixed the present problem and asked for what callers need. Build on it next time by saying all of that in your first reply.
For the call-line lead, knowing where the number came from is what tells her whether the rest of the guide can be trusted.

choices.text: “It's a small thing, and I'll make sure it's right. Callers can always find the current number on the program page, so I really don't think anyone else needs to get involved here.”
choices.consequence: The call-line lead reads the reply and does not answer. A few minutes later, the team lead messages you privately to ask where the number came from. Callers who wrote down the old number still have it, and the old contact list is still in the shared folder.

feedback.text: Keeping a slip in proportion is reasonable, but this reply answers neither of her questions. A stronger move says where the number came from and whether it could be elsewhere.
For a caller waiting on help that is not coming, the program page is not much use if they never think to look. The call-line lead is speaking for them.
What makes a mistake feel smaller when you describe it, and who carries the difference?

decisions.setup: Late Tuesday afternoon, the newer team member asks if you have a minute and steps into a small meeting room with you. “Can I tell you something? Since I started, the colleague from another team keeps shortening my name. I've asked him to stop. He says my name is too hard to say. Yesterday after the huddle, he did it again in front of the call-line staff, and some of them laughed.” The newer team member pauses. “I don't know if it's a big deal. I don't want to make it a thing.”
decisions.prompt: What do you say?

choices.text: “Thanks for telling me. That's not okay, and you don't have to judge how serious it is. Would it help to go over who you could take this to? Your call.”
choices.consequence: He nods slowly. You tell him this stays with you unless he decides otherwise. You go over the options together: the team lead, Human Resources, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, a union representative and the Employee Assistance Program. You mention, honestly, that the team lead supervises the team, so if he tells the team lead, the team lead has to report a concern like this right away to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, and Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division decide how it is classified. He says he wants to think overnight and may contact Human Resources first. You offer to go with him if he would like company. He says he will let you know, and his shoulders drop a little.

feedback.text: You named it as not okay, lifted the burden of judging it, and left the choice with him. Build on it by checking in later in the week, without pushing him toward a decision.
From his side, “I don't want to make it a thing” may be a worry about what happens next. Knowing the options and who decides can make that worry smaller.
If you are ever there when it happens, a short interruption or a work question can redirect the moment, and a check-in afterward keeps him in control.

choices.text: “That's not okay. Supervisors have to act on this kind of thing, so I'll let the team lead know today. That way it gets handled properly and you don't carry it alone.”
choices.consequence: His face changes. “Wait. I didn't say I wanted that.” You realize that once the team lead knows, he has to report a concern like this right away, before the newer team member has decided anything, and Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division will decide how it is classified. The newer team member says he needs to think, and leaves the room more worried than when he came in.

feedback.text: Wanting it handled by someone with authority is a caring, common reaction. As a peer, though, you do not have a supervisor's duty to report, so going to the team lead first takes the decision away from him.
A stronger move lays out the options, including the team lead, and is honest that telling a supervisor starts a report. Then he chooses.
Whose next step is this, and what would help him take it?

choices.text: “That's not okay. I know him a little. I'll find him tomorrow, ask what he was thinking, and tell him to use your full name. He'll listen to me.”
choices.consequence: He looks alarmed. “Please don't. That'll make things worse with that team, and everyone will know I said something.” He says he will handle it himself, thanks you, and leaves. Neither of you has mentioned the other options he has.

feedback.text: Standing up for him is a generous impulse. Going to the colleague from another team on his behalf, without asking, means finding out what happened yourself and acting before he has chosen anything.
From his side, a peer confronting the other colleague could make him visible in exactly the way he was trying to avoid.
Try asking first: “Do you want to do anything about it? Here are the people you could go to, and I can come with you.”

choices.text: “I'm sure he doesn't mean anything by it. He jokes with everyone. Maybe just laugh it off, or ask him again in a friendly way so it doesn't get awkward between teams.”
choices.consequence: He nods and says, “Yeah, maybe.” He does not bring it up again. The following week it happens again in a meeting, and he says nothing. Neither does anyone around him.

feedback.text: Keeping things smooth between teams matters, but this keeps happening after he asked the colleague to stop. State policy lists deliberately mispronouncing a name among its examples, and Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division decide how it is classified. A stronger response says it is not okay and shares the options.
Reaching for good intent is a very common way to calm a hard moment. Intent does not erase the effect, and he came to you because the effect is real.
What did he need to hear to know it was okay to take this further?

practiced: Bringing a dismissed question back to the work without making the person who asked it the topic
Admitting your own uncertainty so others can look again
Handling your own mistake in the present before turning it into a lesson
Giving a plain account of what happened and where it came from
Keeping a colleague's concern in their hands while making the options concrete
Knowing that a supervisor must report a protected-class concern right away, and saying so honestly
this_week: In your next meeting, if a question gets brushed aside, try one sentence that brings it back: “Who can confirm which one applies?”
The next time you find a mistake of your own, tell the people who rely on the work what happened before you fix the cause.
Look up the current contacts for Human Resources, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division and the Employee Assistance Program, so you can share them if someone asks.
When someone questions your work this week, ask one clarifying question before you explain.

simulations.intro: If you work a front desk, a phone line or a schedule, you are often the first to see where a process breaks, and the last to be asked about it. I have found it easy to fix a problem quietly and move on. Here, you handle a teammate’s mistake with a visitor waiting, raise a template problem in a rushed huddle, and decide what to say when a break-room comment turns a process gap into a label.
simulations.title: The Rescheduled Appointment
simulations.learner_role: You are an Office and Administrative Specialist at a DHS front desk. You greet visitors, schedule appointments, and arrange interpreters and accommodations through the scheduling system. You are not a supervisor. Changes to the shared scheduling template, and anything a policy requires, belong to your supervisor or the person or area responsible.
simulations.background: A visitor arrives for a ten o’clock appointment. When you booked it two weeks ago, he asked for an interpreter, and you entered the request. Last week your teammate moved the appointment to today. Now there is no interpreter booked. Looking at the record, you see why: when an appointment is rescheduled in the team’s template, the interpreter request field clears. The visitor is waiting in the lobby, holding his appointment letter. This office’s practice when an interpreter is missing is to offer the visitor a phone interpreter now or a new appointment, whichever he prefers.

decisions.setup: Your teammate comes back from break and sees the record on your screen. “Oh no,” he says. “Did I do that?” The visitor is watching from the lobby. He holds up his letter and points to the line that says an interpreter was requested.
decisions.prompt: What do you do first?

choices.text: Get a phone interpreter on the line and ask the visitor whether to go ahead now or rebook. Then show your teammate how the request field cleared when the date moved.
choices.consequence: With a phone interpreter on the line, the visitor chooses to go ahead now, and the appointment starts twenty minutes late. Your teammate studies the record. “So it wasn’t just me?” “The template cleared it,” you say. “Neither of us thought to re-check it, either.” He writes down the case so he can look at his other reschedules.

feedback.text: You took care of the person waiting before the conversation about how it happened, and you let him choose. Then you showed your teammate the record instead of a verdict. Build on it: the template issue you just found affects more than one appointment, so it needs to reach the person who can change it.
For your teammate, “the field cleared” changes the story from “I failed” to “something in the process let us both down.” That makes him more likely to check, and to tell you next time.

choices.text: Book the phone interpreter for the visitor, fix the record yourself, and tell your teammate not to worry about it, since everyone misses things and he looks upset enough already.
